footnote: [^ch06-lunch-alertness]: Monk et al. (1996) observed a vigilance dip in five of twelve participants even when hourly liquid supplements replaced lunch. Reyner et al. (2012) found greater EEG sleepiness and lane drifting after a heavier lunch in a counterbalanced driving-simulator study of twelve men restricted to five hours' sleep. That meal differed in calories, fat, and carbohydrate, so the study did not isolate carbohydrate as the cause.
references: Monk, T. H., Buysse, D. J., Reynolds, C. F., III, & Kupfer, D. J. (1996). Circadian determinants of the postlunch dip in performance. *Chronobiology International, 13*(2), 123–133. https://doi.org/10.3109/07420529609037076

Reyner, L. A., Wells, S. J., Mortlock, V., & Horne, J. A. (2012). ‘Post-lunch’ sleepiness during prolonged, monotonous driving—Effects of meal size. *Physiology & Behavior, 105*(4), 1088–1091. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.physbeh.2011.11.025
